title: Dylan and the Lock Gate Adventure
markdown:
There was a little duckling named Dylan, with fuzz the colour of a dandelion and eyes that sparkled with more questions than a whole pondful of dragonflies. He loved adventures, though sometimes his bravery wobbled when things did not go as planned. He lived by a pond wide enough to hold the sky, where dragonflies zipped like tiny shimmering jewels and water lilies unfurled their broad green leaves like sleepy dancers stretching in the morning sun.

Dylan’s most special possession was a small sturdy toy boat. He called her the Salty Seagull. He had made her himself, with smooth polished wood that felt just right in his tiny beak, and a brave little sail he had found tangled near the gnarled roots of the old oak at the water’s edge. He loved to push her out onto the shimmering surface and imagine grand voyages, with himself as captain.

One blustery afternoon he gave the Salty Seagull a gentle shove. A particularly strong gust, mischievous and swift, swooped down from the sky. It caught the little sail, filling it like a tiny parachute, and sent her bobbing away faster than Dylan could possibly paddle.

“Oh, no!” His little heart gave a funny panicked thump against his ribs. The Salty Seagull drifted toward the tall reedy part of the pond, where the reeds grew so thick they whispered secrets to the wind, slender stalks swaying like dancers. Beyond those rustling reeds, Dylan knew with a sinking feeling, stood the great mysterious lock gate.

He paddled as fast as his webbed feet could carry him, bright yellow fuzz a blur against the rippling water, but the boat stayed quicker, carried by the playful wind. As he drew closer to the reedy patch, the sounds of the pond seemed to hush, replaced by a quiet rhythmic snip-snap-snip on the breeze.

Sitting on a smooth mossy stone, fingers busy with a length of tough brown twine, was Knurl. Knurl was a knot-maker gnome, and his beard looked exactly like dried reeds woven together, a cascade of earthy browns and pale greens. He was known throughout the pond, and far beyond, for making the most useful and beautiful knots imaginable, each one perfect for its purpose.

Dylan paddled up, his voice trembling a little, like a leaf about to fall. “Excuse me, Mr. Knurl?”

Knurl looked up. His eyes were kind and calm, like the bottom of a clear pool on a sunny day, and they seemed to hold all the patience in the world. “Ah, young Dylan. What troubles your feathers on such a breezy day?”

“My Salty Seagull!” Dylan quacked, pointing a shaky wing. “The wind took her, and she’s drifting toward the lock gate. I can’t reach her there. It looks so big and loud.” The thought of rushing water and enormous metal arms made his fluff prickle.

Knurl stroked his reedy beard thoughtfully, fingers still weaving a complex pattern. “The lock gate. That’s quite a journey through those tall reeds. A bit tricky, with the currents and the stalks. But a lost boat needs a friend, doesn’t it?” He smiled, a gentle reassuring smile that crinkled the corners of his eyes. “I can help you, Dylan. I know a way. Come, follow me. We’ll go carefully.”

Hope fluttered back into Dylan’s chest. He followed Knurl along the edge of the pond. Knurl’s sturdy little legs moved with surprising speed; his quick fingers still fiddled with the twine, tying a neat loop as they went, as if preparing for anything. The reeds rustled around them, a symphony of whispers and sighs. Sunlight dappled through the tall stalks, making shifting patterns of gold and green on the water and the mossy ground. Dylan could hear the distant sound of rushing water now, a deep rumbling that vibrated through the earth. It sounded like a sleepy giant clearing its throat.

They emerged from the thickest reeds into a clearing. Dylan gasped. Before them stood a huge towering structure of metal and stone, far taller than the oldest oak. And there, just nudging gently against its side, bobbing serenely, was the Salty Seagull.

Something else was happening too, something that made the deep rumbling louder. A much bigger boat — a wide barge piled high with colourful crates, a kindly-faced captain waving from its deck — sat in a section of water between two enormous solid gates.

“What’s happening?” Dylan whispered, eyes wide, worries forgotten for a moment.

Knurl pointed with a finger that had a small perfectly tied knot around the tip, like a tiny useful decoration. “The water. It moves up and down, you see. A clever trick to help boats travel where they couldn’t otherwise. When the barge needs to go higher, the gate behind it is closed, and more water is let into this section, filling it up. When it needs to go lower, the water is let out, flowing away.”

He held up the length of twine he had been working. “It’s like this knot.” He created a loose loop. “When the water level is low, the boat sits here.” He showed the loop tight against the lower part of the twine. “Then the gate opens, and the water rises all around it.” He loosened the twine, letting the loop slide upward smoothly. “And then the boat floats up, up, up.”

As Knurl spoke, his voice a calm explanation in the midst of the water’s rumble, Dylan watched with absolute amazement. The barge, with its friendly captain who gave a cheerful toot of the horn, slowly, gently, rose higher and higher within its section of the lock. The Salty Seagull, caught in the same rising water, bobbed along beside it, now much closer to the edge where Dylan stood, within easy reach.

“Look!” cried Dylan. “My boat! She’s coming closer!”

Knurl chuckled, a sound like smooth pebbles rolling in a stream. “Go on, little one. Retrieve your Salty Seagull. She’s waited patiently for you.”

With a happy triumphant quack, Dylan paddled the short distance. He gently nudged his boat toward him with his beak. Not a scratch, though she looked a little damp from her adventure. He held her close, feeling the smooth familiar wood.

“Oh, thank you, Knurl! Thank you for showing me the lock gate. And thank you for saving my Salty Seagull!”

Knurl smiled, eyes crinkling. He wiggled his knotted fingers once, then tucked the twine into his pocket as if the lesson had finished tying itself.

They walked back together. The setting sun painted the sky in orange, pink, and soft purple, reflecting on the calm surface of the pond. Dylan tucked the Salty Seagull safely under his wing. The lock’s rumble faded behind the reeds, and the snip-snap of Knurl’s work did not start up again. Somewhere along the path the little knot on Knurl’s finger had come undone, and Dylan did not ask him to tie it. The water had already shown him how a loop could rise.
